title: Vector Fields
description: Vector fields (OpenStax 6.1, a 40 minute class): drag a probe through radial, rotational, whirlpool, unit, gravitational and gradient fields, release a particle to trace flow lines, and use a live cross-partial readout to test for conservative fields, with many verified examples.

steps.label: What Is a Vector Field?
steps.subtitle: Definition, notation, and Example 1
steps.bodyHtml:
A vector field attaches a vector to every point of its domain. Think of a weather map: at each point of the map, an arrow gives the wind there. Or the surface of a river: at each point, the velocity of the water.

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \(\vec F(x,y)=\langle P(x,y),\,Q(x,y)\rangle=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j\), defined on a region \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^3\): \(\vec F(x,y,z)=\langle P,Q,R\rangle=P\,\mathbf i+Q\,\mathbf j+R\,\mathbf k\), defined on \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3\).

The input is a point, the output is a vector. Compare: a scalar function \(f(x,y)\) outputs a number. \(\vec F\) is continuous if \(P\), \(Q\) (and \(R\)) are. To draw it, put the tail of \(\vec F(x,y)\) at the point \((x,y)\).

Example 1. \(\vec F(x,y)=(2y^2+x-4)\,\mathbf i+\cos x\,\mathbf j\). Find \(\vec F(0,-1)\)\(P(0,-1)=2(1)+0-4=-2\) and \(Q(0,-1)=\cos0=1\). So \(\vec F(0,-1)=-2\,\mathbf i+\mathbf j\), drawn with its tail at \((0,-1)\).
Checkpoint 1. \(\vec G(x,y)=x^2y\,\mathbf i-(x+y)\,\mathbf j\). Find \(\vec G(-2,3)\)\(x^2y=4\cdot3=12\) and \(-(x+y)=-(1)=-1\): \(\ \vec G(-2,3)=12\,\mathbf i-\mathbf j\).
What is the domain of \(\vec F=\Big\langle\dfrac{y}{x^2+y^2},\ \dfrac{-x}{x^2+y^2}\Big\rangle\)?Every point except the origin: \(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\).

Plan: radial and rotational fields, unit fields, fields in space, gradient (conservative) fields, how to test for them, flow lines, and building fields. Every picture below is live: drag the red point.

steps.label: Radial Fields
steps.subtitle: Example 2 and Checkpoint 2
steps.bodyHtml:
A radial field points directly away from (or toward) the origin, with a magnitude that depends only on the distance from the origin. Each vector is perpendicular to the circle centered at the origin through its tail.

Switch between \(F=\langle \tfrac x2,\tfrac y2\rangle\) (Example 2) and \(G=\langle -x^3,-y^3\rangle\) (Checkpoint 2). Drag the red point and watch the vector there. Arrow lengths are scaled to fit the picture, so read the exact vector in the readout.

\(F(x,y)=\langle\tfrac x2,\tfrac y2\rangle\). Compute \(F(4,0)\), \(F(0,-2)\), \(F(2,2)\)\(\langle2,0\rangle,\ \langle0,-1\rangle,\ \langle1,1\rangle\). Each points away from the origin.
How does \(\|F\|\) behave?\(\|F\|=\tfrac12\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\): zero at the origin and growing linearly with distance.
Show \(F\) is perpendicular to the circle through \((x,y)\). A tangent vector there is \(\langle-y,x\rangle\)\(F\cdot\langle-y,x\rangle=-\tfrac{xy}2+\tfrac{xy}2=0\). Yes: radial means perpendicular to the circles.
\(G=\langle-x^3,-y^3\rangle\): inward or outward? Compare \(\|G\|\) at \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\)Inward (it points opposite to \(\langle x,y\rangle\)). \(\|G(1,1)\|=\sqrt2\) but \(\|G(2,2)\|=8\sqrt2\): the magnitude grows like the cube of the position, much faster than \(F\).

steps.label: Rotational Fields and Whirlpools
steps.subtitle: Examples 3, 4, 5 and Checkpoints 3, 4
steps.bodyHtml:
A rotational field is tangent to circles centered at the origin, all turning the same way, with magnitude depending only on the distance. Press Release particle: it moves with the field, \(\dfrac{d\vec r}{dt}=\vec F(\vec r)\), and traces its path.

A: \(\langle y,-x\rangle\) (Example 3). B: \(\langle-2y,2x\rangle\) (Checkpoint 3). W: \(\Big\langle\tfrac{y}{x^2+y^2},\tfrac{-x}{x^2+y^2}\Big\rangle\) (Example 4, a whirlpool).

A. Show the vectors are tangent to circles\(\langle x,y\rangle\cdot\langle y,-x\rangle=xy-xy=0\): perpendicular to the radius, so tangent to the circle.
A. Direction of rotation and \(\|F\|\)Clockwise (at \((1,0)\) it is \(\langle0,-1\rangle\), pointing down). \(\|F\|=\sqrt{y^2+x^2}\), growing with distance.
B. Describe itRotational, counterclockwise (at \((1,0)\) it is \(\langle0,2\rangle\)), with magnitude \(2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), twice as strong as the field \(\langle-y,x\rangle\).
W. Find \(\|F\|\). What happens near the origin?\(\|F\|=\dfrac{\sqrt{y^2+x^2}}{x^2+y^2}=\dfrac1{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\to\infty\) as \((x,y)\to(0,0)\). The field is undefined at the origin, and the vectors get huge and turn fast near it: a whirlpool.
Example 5. Water velocity \(\vec v=\Big\langle\dfrac{-2y}{x^2+y^2},\dfrac{2x}{x^2+y^2}\Big\rangle\) m/s. Find the speed at \((1,-1)\)\(\vec v(1,-1)=\langle\tfrac{2}{2},\tfrac{2}{2}\rangle=\langle1,1\rangle\). Speed \(=\|\vec v\|=\sqrt2\approx1.41\) m/s.
Checkpoint 4. \(\vec v=\langle4|x|,\,1\rangle\) m/s. Speed at \((2,3)\)\(\vec v(2,3)=\langle8,1\rangle\), speed \(\sqrt{65}\approx8.06\) m/s. (Only \(x\) matters; this field is neither radial nor rotational.)

steps.label: Unit Vector Fields
steps.subtitle: Example 6 and Checkpoint 5: normalizing
steps.bodyHtml:
A unit vector field has \(\|\vec F\|=1\) everywhere: only the direction is kept. Given any field with \(\vec F\neq\vec0\), the normalized field is \(\dfrac{\vec F}{\|\vec F\|}\).

Press Unit vectors on field F: all the arrows become the same length, and the picture becomes the field G.

Example 6. Show \(G=\Big\langle\dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}},\dfrac{-x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\Big\rangle\) is a unit field\(\|G\|^2=\dfrac{y^2}{x^2+y^2}+\dfrac{x^2}{x^2+y^2}=1\). So \(\|G\|=1\) at every point except the origin. \(G\) is \(\langle y,-x\rangle\) divided by its length \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\).
Checkpoint 5. Is \(\vec F=\langle-y,x\rangle\) a unit field?No: \(\|\vec F\|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), which is \(1\) only on the unit circle. Its unit version is \(\dfrac{\langle-y,x\rangle}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\).
Normalize \(\vec F=\langle x,2\rangle\) and evaluate at \((3,2)\)\(\|\vec F\|=\sqrt{x^2+4}\). At \((3,2)\): \(\vec F=\langle3,2\rangle\), \(\|\vec F\|=\sqrt{13}\), unit vector \(\dfrac1{\sqrt{13}}\langle3,2\rangle\).
Why would we want a unit field?When only the direction matters (flow direction, a compass heading), and it makes a plot readable when the true magnitudes vary wildly (near the whirlpool).

steps.label: Vector Fields in Space
steps.subtitle: Examples 7, 8: \(\mathbb{R}^3\) and gravity
steps.bodyHtml:
The same idea with three components. Example 7. \(\vec F=\langle1,1,z\rangle\).

\(\vec F\) in the \(xy\)-plane (\(z=0\))\(\langle1,1,0\rangle\) everywhere: horizontal vectors, all alike.
\(\vec F(0,0,2)\) and \(\vec F(0,0,-2)\)\(\langle1,1,2\rangle\) (tilting up) and \(\langle1,1,-2\rangle\) (tilting down): the farther from the plane, the steeper the tilt.
Checkpoint 6. \(\vec G=\langle2,z^2,1\rangle\) at \((0,0,2)\) and \((5,-1,0)\)\(\langle2,4,1\rangle\) and \(\langle2,0,1\rangle\). The vector does not depend on \(x\) or \(y\) at all.

Example 8 (Newton's law of gravitation). A mass \(m_1\) at the origin pulls a mass \(m_2\) at \((x,y,z)\) with the force field

$$\vec F(x,y,z)=-\frac{G\,m_1m_2}{r^2}\,\hat{\mathbf r}=-G\,m_1m_2\,\frac{\langle x,y,z\rangle}{r^3},\qquad r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}.$$
Why is it radial? Which way does it point?It is a negative multiple of the position vector \(\langle x,y,z\rangle\): always toward the origin.
Show \(\|\vec F\|=\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\)\(\|\langle x,y,z\rangle\|=r\), so \(\|\vec F\|=Gm_1m_2\cdot\dfrac r{r^3}=\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}\): an inverse-square law.
Take \(Gm_1m_2=1\). Find \(\vec F(1,2,2)\) and its magnitude\(r=3\): \(\vec F=-\dfrac{\langle1,2,2\rangle}{27}\) and \(\|\vec F\|=\dfrac19\).
Now double the distance: \(\vec F(2,4,4)\)\(r=6\), \(\|\vec F\|=\tfrac1{36}\): doubling the distance divides the force by \(4\).

Here is the slice \(z=0\) of this field with \(Gm_1m_2=1\). Move the probe inward and watch \(\|\vec F\|\) blow up like \(1/r^2\); the arrows are capped in length so the picture stays readable.

steps.label: Gradient Fields
steps.subtitle: Example 9, Checkpoint 8, and the definition of conservative
steps.bodyHtml:
For a scalar function \(f\), the gradient \(\nabla f=\langle f_x,f_y\rangle\) is a vector field. A field \(\vec F\) is a gradient field (or conservative) if \(\vec F=\nabla f\) for some \(f\); then \(f\) is a potential function for \(\vec F\).

Example 9. \(f(x,y)=x^2y^2\). The grey curves are level curves of \(f\), the green one passes through the red point. The arrows are \(\nabla f\).

Compute \(\nabla f\)\(\nabla f=\langle2xy^2,\ 2x^2y\rangle\). At \((1,2)\): \(\langle8,4\rangle\). At \((1,1)\): \(\langle2,2\rangle\).
Drag the point along a level curve. How is \(\nabla f\) related to that curve?\(\nabla f\) is perpendicular to the level curve through the point, and it points toward larger values of \(f\).
Where are the arrows longest?Where the level curves are close together (steep parts of the graph of \(f\)), and \(\nabla f=\vec0\) on the axes where \(f\) is flat.
Checkpoint 8. Gradient field of \(f=\sin x\cos y\)\(\nabla f=\langle\cos x\cos y,\ -\sin x\sin y\rangle\).
Gradient of \(f=\tfrac12(x^2+y^2)\). Which field from step 2 is it?\(\langle x,y\rangle\): the radial field \(\vec F\) (up to the factor \(\tfrac12\)) of Example 2 is conservative, with level curves that are circles.

Some books (physics) define the field as \(-\nabla f\). Same idea, opposite sign.

steps.label: Verifying a Potential Function
steps.subtitle: Examples 10, 11, Theorem 6.1 and Checkpoints 9, 10
steps.bodyHtml:
To check that \(f\) is a potential for \(\vec F\), compute \(\nabla f\) and compare with \(\vec F\), component by component.

Example 10. Is \(f=x^2yz-\sin(xy)\) a potential for \(\vec F=\langle2xyz-y\cos(xy),\ x^2z-x\cos(xy),\ x^2y\rangle\)?\(f_x=2xyz-y\cos(xy)\), \(f_y=x^2z-x\cos(xy)\), \(f_z=x^2y\). All three match. Yes.
Example 11. Is \(f=\tfrac{x^2y}2-\tfrac{y^2}2\) a potential for \(\vec v=\langle xy,\ \tfrac{x^2}2-y\rangle\)?\(f_x=xy\), \(f_y=\tfrac{x^2}2-y\). Yes.
Checkpoint 10. \(f=x^3y^2+1\) and \(\vec F=\langle3x^2y^2,\ 2x^3y\rangle\)\(f_x=3x^2y^2\), \(f_y=2x^3y\). Yes. (The \(+1\) disappears when we differentiate.)
Try one that fails: is \(f=x^2y\) a potential for \(\vec F=\langle2xy,\ xy\rangle\)?\(f_x=2xy\) matches, but \(f_y=x^2\neq xy\). No.
A 3D one: \(f=x^2\cos(yz)+y^2z^2\) and \(\vec F=\langle2x\cos(yz),\ -x^2z\sin(yz)+2yz^2,\ -x^2y\sin(yz)+2y^2z\rangle\)\(f_x=2x\cos(yz)\), \(f_y=-x^2z\sin(yz)+2yz^2\), \(f_z=-x^2y\sin(yz)+2y^2z\). All match. Yes.

Theorem 6.1 (uniqueness). If \(\vec F\) is conservative on an open, connected domain and \(\nabla f=\nabla g=\vec F\), then \(f=g+C\) for some constant \(C\).

Why? Look at \(h=f-g\)\(\nabla h=\vec F-\vec F=\vec0\), so all partials of \(h\) vanish and \(h\) is constant on a connected domain. (On a domain in two separate pieces, the constant could differ on each piece.)
Another potential for Example 11?Any \(\tfrac{x^2y}2-\tfrac{y^2}2+C\), for example with \(C=5\).

steps.label: The Cross-Partial Test
steps.subtitle: Theorem 6.2 and Examples 12, 13
steps.bodyHtml:
Theorem 6.2. If \(\vec F=\langle P,Q\rangle\) is conservative with continuous first partials, then

$$\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}.$$

In \(\mathbb{R}^3\): \(P_y=Q_x\), \(\ Q_z=R_y\), \(\ R_x=P_z\). The reason: \(P=f_x\) and \(Q=f_y\), so \(P_y=f_{xy}=f_{yx}=Q_x\) (Clairaut).

Pick a field, drag the point, and read both partials. A and W were seen before; B is \(\langle y,x\rangle\); C is \(\langle2xy+3,\ x^2+4y\rangle\).

Example 12. \(\vec F=\langle y,-x\rangle\). Conservative?\(P_y=1\) but \(Q_x=-1\). Not equal, so not conservative. (Consistent with the picture: the field circles around, and a potential would have to increase all the way around a loop.)
Example 13. \(\vec F=\langle7,-2,x^3\rangle\)\(R_x=3x^2\) but \(P_z=0\). Not equal: not conservative.
Checkpoint 12. \(\vec G=\langle y,x,xyz\rangle\)\(R_y=xz\) but \(Q_z=0\). Not conservative. (The pair \(P_y=1=Q_x\) passes, but one failure is enough.)
Field B: \(\langle y,x\rangle\). Test it, then guess a potential\(P_y=1=Q_x\). Passes, and \(f=xy\) works: \(\nabla(xy)=\langle y,x\rangle\).
Field C: test it and find a potential\(P_y=2x=Q_x\). Integrate \(P\) in \(x\): \(f=x^2y+3x+g(y)\). Then \(f_y=x^2+g'(y)=x^2+4y\), so \(g=2y^2\) and \(f=x^2y+3x+2y^2\). (This procedure is Section 6.3.)

Warning: only a necessary condition. It can prove a field is not conservative, but not that it is.

Field W (whirlpool): compute \(P_y\) and \(Q_x\)\(P_y=\dfrac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}=Q_x\) at every point of its domain. The test passes, yet W is not conservative: around the unit circle its circulation is \(\int_0^{2\pi}(-1)\,dt=-2\pi\neq0\), while a conservative field gives \(0\) around a closed loop. The hole at the origin is the culprit. Next lesson: line integrals.

steps.label: Flow Lines
steps.subtitle: A vector field as a velocity field
steps.bodyHtml:
If \(\vec F\) is a velocity field, a particle dropped in the flow follows a flow line: a curve \(\vec r(t)\) with \(\vec{r}'(t)=\vec F(\vec r(t))\). Its velocity at each moment is the field vector at its position. Pick a field, drag the point to choose the starting position, and release.

A: \(\langle y,-x\rangle\). E: \(\langle x,y\rangle\) (radial). S: \(\langle x,-y\rangle\) (a "saddle", the field H of the matching exercise in step 10).

Verify that \(\vec r(t)=\langle\cos t,\,-\sin t\rangle\) is a flow line of A\(\vec{r}'=\langle-\sin t,-\cos t\rangle\) and \(\vec F(\vec r)=\langle y,-x\rangle=\langle-\sin t,-\cos t\rangle\). Equal. The path is the unit circle, traveled clockwise.
Verify that \(\vec r(t)=\langle e^t,\,2e^t\rangle\) is a flow line of E\(\vec{r}'=\langle e^t,2e^t\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle=\vec F(\vec r)\). The path is the ray \(y=2x\) leaving the origin, faster and faster.
Verify that \(\vec r(t)=\langle e^t,\,e^{-t}\rangle\) is a flow line of S. What curve is it?\(\vec{r}'=\langle e^t,-e^{-t}\rangle=\langle x,-y\rangle\). \(\ xy=e^te^{-t}=1\): the hyperbola \(y=1/x\). Release a particle from \((1,1)\) to see it.
Solve for the flow line of E through \((1,2)\) at \(t=0\)\(x'=x\), \(y'=y\) give \(x=c_1e^t\), \(y=c_2e^t\). Initial point: \(c_1=1\), \(c_2=2\). So \(\vec r(t)=\langle e^t,2e^t\rangle\), the one we verified.
In field A, can two flow lines cross?No. At a crossing point they would need two different velocities, but \(\vec F\) has exactly one vector there.

steps.label: Build It and Match It
steps.subtitle: Constructing fields, and the matching exercise
steps.bodyHtml:
Constructing. Write a formula for each field.

(a) A unit field at every point pointing toward \((1,0)\) (Exercise 21)The vector from \((x,y)\) to \((1,0)\) is \(\langle1-x,-y\rangle\), with length \(\sqrt{(x-1)^2+y^2}\). So \(\vec F=\dfrac{\langle1-x,\,-y\rangle}{\sqrt{(x-1)^2+y^2}}\), undefined at \((1,0)\) itself.
(b) Counterclockwise rotational field with constant magnitude \(3\)Tangent direction \(\langle-y,x\rangle\), normalized and times \(3\): \(\vec F=\dfrac{3\langle-y,x\rangle}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\).
(c) A radial field pointing away from the origin with magnitude \(r^2\)Direction \(\dfrac{\langle x,y\rangle}{r}\) times \(r^2\): \(\vec F=r\langle x,y\rangle=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,\langle x,y\rangle\).

Matching. Let \(F=\langle x,y\rangle\), \(G=\langle-y,x\rangle\), \(H=\langle x,-y\rangle\). First predict the picture of each combination, then press its button.

\(F+G\)\(\langle x-y,\ x+y\rangle\): outward from \(F\) plus counterclockwise from \(G\), an outward counterclockwise spiral.
\(-F+G\)\(\langle-x-y,\ x-y\rangle\): inward plus counterclockwise, an inward spiral.
\(F+H\)\(\langle2x,0\rangle\): purely horizontal, pointing away from the \(y\)-axis on both sides. The \(y\)-components cancel.
\(G+H\)\(\langle x-y,\ x-y\rangle=(x-y)\langle1,1\rangle\): every vector is parallel to \(\langle1,1\rangle\), zero along the line \(y=x\), flipping direction across it.

steps.label: Summary
steps.subtitle: The one-page version
steps.bodyHtml:
Vector fieldA vector \(\vec F(x,y)=\langle P,Q\rangle\) (or \(\langle P,Q,R\rangle\)) at each point. Draw it with the tail at the point.
Radial / rotationalRadial \(\parallel\langle x,y\rangle\) (perpendicular to circles). Rotational \(\parallel\langle-y,x\rangle\) (tangent to circles). Magnitude depends only on \(r\).
Unit field\(\vec F/\|\vec F\|\): only the direction.
Gravity\(\vec F=-Gm_1m_2\langle x,y,z\rangle/r^3\): radial inward, magnitude \(Gm_1m_2/r^2\).
Conservative\(\vec F=\nabla f\). Potentials differ by a constant (Thm 6.1). \(\nabla f\perp\) level curves.
Test\(P_y=Q_x\) (and \(Q_z=R_y\), \(R_x=P_z\)) is necessary. Failing it proves "not conservative"; passing it proves nothing by itself (the whirlpool passes).
Flow line\(\vec{r}'(t)=\vec F(\vec r(t))\).

Homework: OpenStax 6.1 Checkpoints 6.1 to 6.12 and exercises on sketching fields (5 to 14), gradient fields (15 to 20), constructing fields (21 to 25), the gradient test (26), electric fields (28, 29), flow lines (30, 31) and matching (32 to 38). Next: line integrals.

Vector fields in space 4 min; 6. Gradient fields 4 min; 7. Verifying a potential 4 min; 8. The cross-partial test 5 min; 9. Flow lines 3 min; 10. Build it and match it 4 min; 11. Summary 1 min.
